questions.q: What does this lesson say actually makes a set of controls "defense in depth," as opposed to just a long feature list?
options: Having the maximum number of security features enabled, regardless of how they relate to each other
Using only Salesforce Shield features and nothing else
The layers being independent -- each failing for a different reason or under different conditions, so one root cause can't take all of them out at once
Requiring every user to have the same profile
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction is independence: ten controls that all share one underlying assumption are one layer with ten names, not real depth. Real depth comes from layers that fail for different reasons.

questions.q: In the worked phishing example, which layer actually failed, and which layers were what limited the damage?
options: The field-level layer failed; nothing else mattered
Every layer failed simultaneously, since one compromised credential defeats all controls at once
No layer failed -- the attacker never actually logged in
The network/identity layer failed (credentials were phished); the authorization, field-level, and monitoring/response layers each limited the resulting damage
questions.explain: The phishing attack succeeded at the network/identity layer, but the authorization layer (scoped Account access), the field-level layer (encrypted/FLS-protected credit limit field), and the monitoring/response layer (Transaction Security step-up challenge) each independently limited how much damage that single failure caused.

questions.q: Per this lesson's mindset, what question should an architect ask about every individual control in the stack?
options: Assuming this control eventually fails, what does the next layer do about it?
Is this control the single most important one, so the others can be skipped?
Does this control cost the least to implement?
Can this control be removed without anyone noticing?
questions.explain: Defense in depth assumes every control eventually fails and asks what the next layer does in response -- if the honest answer is "nothing, the breach is now total," the design doesn't actually have depth.

questions.q: In the layer table, which pair of controls belongs to the "field-level and data protection" layer specifically, as distinct from the authorization (object/record) layer above it?
options: Login IP ranges and multi-factor authentication
Field-Level Security and Shield Platform Encryption
Profiles and Org-Wide Defaults
Setup Audit Trail and Event Monitoring
questions.explain: Field-Level Security and Shield Platform Encryption sit at the innermost data-protection layer, stopping a user who already has legitimate record access from seeing specific fields they shouldn't -- a different job than object/record authorization above it.

questions.q: In the Lab's modified scenario, the sales rep's profile is changed from scoped Account access to "View All Data." What does this change illustrate about defense in depth?
options: It illustrates that the monitoring/response layer becomes unnecessary once authorization is removed
It illustrates that "View All Data" has no effect on how much an attacker with a phished login can see

It illustrates that removing one layer's independence (here, authorization) removes the protection that layer was providing, so the same single credential compromise now causes more damage even though the other layers are unchanged
It illustrates that defense in depth requires removing field-level security once object-level access is broad
questions.explain: Defense in depth only works if each layer actually holds independently -- over-permissioning the authorization layer removes one of the layers that was limiting the damage from the identity-layer failure, which is exactly why Lesson 2's least privilege matters to this lesson's model.
